rhs_question_text: A school builds a simple processor for an interactive museum exhibit. Describe the fetch stage of its Fetch–Decode–Execute cycle, referring to relevant registers and buses. [4]
rhs_answer_points_draft: The PC stores the address of the next instruction. The address is copied to MAR and sent along the address bus; the control unit signals memory read on the control bus; memory returns the instruction across the data bus into MDR, then CIR; the PC advances.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Up to four distinct accurate steps involving PC, MAR, address bus, control bus, data bus, MDR, CIR and PC increment; avoid giving several marks for one identical step.

rhs_question_text: An instruction in the exhibit's program jumps to a new memory location. Which processor register changes during that branch? [1]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Program Counter (PC).
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for PC / Program Counter.

rhs_question_text: The processor in a classroom robot overlaps parts of consecutive instructions through pipelining. Explain three ways this can improve its performance. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: It may fetch the next instruction while decoding/executing an earlier one. This overlaps instruction stages, reduces unused CPU-unit time and increases throughput.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for overlapping stages, one for higher instruction throughput, one for less idle hardware/waiting. Do not give credit for a claim that a single entire FDE cycle becomes faster.

rhs_question_text:
A coding club attempts an LMC program that should display the first five Fibonacci values, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3. The club's faulty program is shown. Trace it exactly and give the five printed values. [3]

LOOP LDA COUNT
BRZ STOP
LDA FIRST
OUT
LDA SECOND
STA FIRST
LDA SECOND
ADD SECOND
STA SECOND
LDA COUNT
SUB ONE
STA COUNT
BRA LOOP
STOP HLT
FIRST DAT 0
SECOND DAT 1
COUNT DAT 5
ONE DAT 1
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Three marks grouped as 0 correct (1), the consecutive middle values 1,2,4 (1), final 8 and no extra values (1).

rhs_question_text:
The coding club rewrites its Fibonacci code. Complete the four one-instruction blanks below so the five values printed become 0, 1, 1, 2, 3. [4]

START LDA COUNT
BRZ FINISH
LDA FIRST
OUT
LDA FIRST
ADD SECOND
________
________
________
________
STA SECOND
LDA COUNT
SUB ONE
STA COUNT
BRA START
FINISH HLT
FIRST DAT 0
SECOND DAT 1
NEXT DAT 0
COUNT DAT 5
ONE DAT 1
rhs_answer_points_draft: Four blanks, in order: STA NEXT; LDA SECOND; STA FIRST; LDA NEXT.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark per correct LMC instruction in its correct position. The rewritten RHS program uses FIRST, SECOND and NEXT instead of the OCR source's data labels.

rhs_question_text: In addition to direct memory addressing, name three other addressing modes a processor might use. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Immediate, indirect and indexed.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for each of immediate, indirect and indexed; do not credit direct.

rhs_question_text: A manufacturer wants software to control specialist hardware with little memory. Give two distinct reasons it might choose assembly language rather than a high-level language. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Direct access to hardware/registers; tightly controlled memory/CPU-resource use; platform-specific instructions; potentially quicker translation; lack of a high-level compiler for the target processor.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for each distinct supported reason. Performance claims need a comparison rather than a generic assertion of speed.

rhs_question_text: A design studio upgrades the RAM in computers used for large graphics projects. Explain how this could improve performance. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: More currently running programs and working data can be held in RAM, reducing reliance on much slower virtual memory/secondary-storage swapping and the risk of thrashing.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Up to three separate points: more active working data in RAM; less use of disk virtual memory; RAM access faster; less swapping/thrashing.

rhs_question_text: A conservation team clips tiny monitoring devices to migrating birds to track movement and conditions. Name one suitable input sensor and explain one specific measurement it would provide. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: GPS receiver for position/route; accelerometer for motion or acceleration; temperature sensor for environmental temperature; other appropriate input sensors with context-linked uses.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for a suitable sensor, one for a valid linked measurement. An unsuitable output device earns no follow-through use mark.

rhs_question_text: A bird tracker is lightweight, runs from a small battery and may receive shocks in flight. Explain TWO separate advantages of using flash secondary storage. Link each advantage to this particular device. [4]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Flash has no moving parts, so impact will not damage moving media; uses relatively little power, helping battery life; compact and light, reducing load on the bird; fast read/write useful for continuous logging.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Two supported property-and-consequence pairs, up to 2 marks each. A bare claim of storage capacity does not meet the source's allowed reasons.

rhs_question_text: A wildlife field tablet stores firmware in ROM. Describe three actions that its BIOS/start-up firmware can perform before normal use begins. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Contains initial start-up instructions; reads configuration; tests/initialises peripherals with POST; reports detected hardware errors; identifies the boot device; loads bootstrap/kernel/OS.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for each distinct valid start-up activity, maximum three. A bare 'boots the tablet' is too vague.

rhs_question_text: A portable tracker uses some ROM to retain security configuration and cryptographic keys. Explain why ROM is suitable for storing such important information. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: ROM provides non-volatile persistent storage of security material and can prevent ordinary programs from altering essential keys or security settings.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for storing important security/firmware information; one for the value of preserving it and preventing ordinary alteration. Equivalent accepted ROM applications may be credited when correctly developed.

rhs_question_text: A shared college workstation is used by several pupils, and has printers, files and user accounts. Describe TWO different operating-system functions other than interrupt handling or CPU scheduling. Give a concrete example for each. [4]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Memory management allocates/releases RAM or coordinates paging. File management finds, stores or moves files. Device management supports peripherals/drivers. User/security management controls accounts or resource permissions. User interface allows users to interact with the computer.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Up to two distinct OS functions, each worth a correct role (1) plus a specific example or development (1), four total. Do not credit scheduling or interrupt-handling.

rhs_question_text:
A school server uses several process schedulers: Round Robin (RR), First Come First Served (FCFS), Shortest Job First (SJF), Shortest Remaining Time (SRT) and Multi-level Feedback Queue (MLFQ). Match each numbered description with the correct abbreviated scheduler.
1. The job with least remaining work is chosen and a running job can be interrupted by a newer shorter job.
2. Each ready job receives a repeated fixed-length CPU time slice.
3. Jobs can be placed in and move between priority queues according to behaviour.
4. Jobs run in order of arrival.
5. The waiting job with smallest total expected duration runs until completion. [5]
rhs_answer_points_draft: 1 SRT; 2 RR; 3 MLFQ; 4 FCFS; 5 SJF.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for each correct matching, maximum five. Each scheduler must match the specific description.

rhs_question_text:
An international wildlife programme is designing a web dashboard for volunteers working across countries with different languages and cultural practices. The dashboard uses symbols, status colours, charts and messages.

Discuss how its user interface should handle differences in language and writing direction, the cultural meaning of colours and symbols, and character sets. Explain ways to reduce misunderstanding and allow the interface to be adapted for different cultures. [9]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Support Unicode and fonts for required scripts; translations and right-to-left reading layouts where appropriate; adapt date/number units and text length; avoid assuming identical meaning of symbols/hand gestures/icons or status colours (for example white or red); select culturally appropriate graphics and conduct local user testing; allow regional customisation. Keep focus on culture, not generic colour-blindness as a substitute.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Nine-mark teacher-assessed levels: high 7–9 detailed, balanced culturally relevant and justified; middle 4–6 sound but underdeveloped; low 1–3 limited; zero for nothing appropriate. Don't award a fixed mark for each named buzzword.

rhs_question_text:
A small theatre company needs software for different office tasks. For each task, give the most suitable TYPE of application software (not a product brand):
1. Creating an original logo.
2. Writing appointment letters to performers.
3. Calculating monthly income and expenditure.
4. Storing, editing and querying audience membership records.
5. Laying out illustrated publicity leaflets for printing. [5]
rhs_answer_points_draft: 1 graphics/image editing; 2 word processing; 3 spreadsheet or accounting; 4 database management; 5 desktop publishing (DTP).
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark per suitable application software category, up to five. Do not award a brand name alone without the correct software type.

rhs_question_text: The theatre company runs its office applications in virtual machines on a central server, accessed from thin clients. State one advantage of this arrangement. [1]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Centralised management; reduced hardware required at desk; virtual machines can be recreated after infection; improved isolation; resources can be allocated flexibly.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for one valid benefit linked to virtual machines/centralised server, not a vague 'faster'.

rhs_question_text: An employee types new names and dates into a thin-client application. Those text changes travel over the network to a server. Explain why lossless compression is preferable to lossy compression for sending the text. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Lossless compression reduces the amount of data transmitted while allowing the exact original text/characters to be reconstructed; lossy compression permanently discards information and could corrupt names or dates.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Three valid developed points from no irreversible loss, complete reconstruction, preserved text integrity/accuracy, risks of unreadable or incorrect text under lossy. One idea repeated cannot earn several marks.

rhs_question_text: A programmer combines separately compiled source modules with reusable library code when building an application. Describe the purpose of the linker. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: A linker connects compiled modules and required library references, resolving addresses/external references and producing a linked executable image.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for linking code/modules/libraries and one for the executable output or resolution of required references.

rhs_question_text: Before an employee runs the theatre application's executable file, the operating system must prepare it. Describe what a loader does. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: The OS loader loads the executable code and required libraries from secondary storage into main memory so the application can be run.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for loading the program/executable into memory, one for describing its secondary-storage source, OS responsibility or required libraries.

rhs_question_text: A meteorological sensor represents a signed reading using eight-bit two's complement. Convert the denary value −124 into an eight-bit two's-complement binary word. [1]
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for the exact 8-bit pattern 10000100.

rhs_question_text: Give one alternative format (other than two's complement) that can represent a negative binary integer. [1]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Sign-and-magnitude or one's complement.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for either valid alternative.

rhs_question_text: A digital controller stores a colour code as denary 298. Convert it to hexadecimal, showing your working. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: 298 = 1×256 + 2×16 + 10, giving hexadecimal 12A.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for 12 as the first two hex digits, one for the final A in the correct order; 12A is fully correct.

rhs_question_text:
A scientific model stores a normalised binary floating-point number using an eight-bit signed two's-complement mantissa and a four-bit signed two's-complement exponent. The stored pattern is:
Mantissa: 10011101
Exponent: 0110
Using the binary point immediately after the sign bit, convert the stored number into denary and show the intermediate calculation. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Exponent 0110 represents +6. Mantissa 10011101 equals −0.7734375 as a signed binary fraction. Multiplying by 2^6 gives −49.5. Equivalently, shifting the mantissa six places yields signed binary 1001110.1, with value −49.5.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for exponent +6 / right binary-point shift of six, one for correct signed mantissa conversion/working, one for final −49.5. Correct final answer with valid binary working can earn full credit; denary-only unsupported guesses do not.

rhs_question_text: An environmental data logger stores a positive quantity in an unnormalised signed floating-point form: eight-bit two's-complement mantissa 00001011 and four-bit two's-complement exponent 0111. Re-express this value as a normalised floating-point number in the SAME eight-plus-four-bit format. Show the mantissa shifts and adjusted exponent. [4]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Normalise positive mantissa until it starts with 01: shift 00001011 left by three positions to 01011000. Decrease the exponent 7 by 3 to 4, written 0100. Final: 01011000 0100.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for reducing exponent by three to 4; one for the mantissa starting 01011...; one for the completed eight-bit mantissa 01011000; one for four-bit exponent 0100. Correct two fields with valid binary working may earn all four.

rhs_question_text:
An eight-bit unsigned counter receives two binary inputs. Add the following eight-bit binary values, showing column carries. [2]
  00110111
+ 10011001
----------
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for 1101 0000, one for correct binary carry working. Source guidance requires visible carries; denary-only working earns no binary-method credit.

rhs_question_text: An equipment store has an alarm with four Boolean inputs: A is front door motion; B is rear door motion; C is the armed switch; D is a maintenance test switch. The siren sounds when either sensor detects motion, the system is armed and test mode is OFF. Draw a circuit using only two-input AND/OR gates and one NOT gate. Label all inputs and siren output S. [4]
rhs_answer_points_draft: S = (A OR B) AND C AND (NOT D). One solution: OR(A,B), NOT(D), AND(OR_result,C), AND(previous_result,NOT_D).
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Four marks for correctly applying OR to sensors, C as required condition, inverted D, and overall AND/output. An extra unnecessary gate limits the original source mark; three-input gates should not be substituted.

rhs_question_text: Simplify (NOT A) OR (NOT B) using a De Morgan transformation. [1]
rhs_answer_points_draft: NOT (A AND B).
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for equivalent ¬(A ∧ B), correctly grouping both inputs.

rhs_question_text: Simplify NOT (NOT B) using double negation. [1]
rhs_answer_points_draft: B.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for B.

rhs_question_text: Use Boolean distribution to simplify (A OR B) AND (A OR C). [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: A OR (B AND C).
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for standalone A, one for OR of B AND C. Accept equivalent Boolean syntax.

rhs_question_text: A new chain of independent bookshops wants customers to find its website easily in search results. Discuss how web crawlers and search indexing work, how PageRank-style link analysis can influence the order of results, and ways the bookshop could improve its pages and incoming links. Evaluate how important these methods would be in competing with larger shops. [12]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Crawlers follow hyperlinks and collect page terms/structure into search indexes. A search engine looks in its index, not the entire live web each time. Link-based ranking represents pages/links as directed edges, and inbound links from reputable/important pages can have more influence. Relevant titles/headings/content, good navigability, and genuine inbound links help discovery; rankings depend on many factors and a new shop cannot guarantee first place.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Teacher holistic marking: detailed, contextual, balanced index/PageRank evaluation 9–12; sound application 5–8; basic response 1–4; nothing valid 0. No naive auto scoring.

rhs_question_text:
An online bookshop runs some tasks in the visitor's browser and others on a server. Label each as CLIENT or SERVER:
1. Loading/rendering the HTML page in the browser.
2. Applying CSS to the HTML in the browser.
3. Checking a required surname field with browser JavaScript before submission.
4. Running a database query to check the stock count for a selected book. [4]
rhs_answer_points_draft: CLIENT, CLIENT, CLIENT, SERVER.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One correct classification per row, four total. Real implementations should also validate submitted data on the server.

rhs_question_text: A customer's phone and the bookshop web server use standard protocols such as TCP/IP and HTTP. Explain what a network protocol is and why agreed standards help their different devices communicate. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: A protocol is a collection of agreed rules governing network data transfer. Shared protocols make communication predictable and interoperable between systems using different hardware/operating systems.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for rules (plural) of communication, one for standardisation/interoperability/predictable data format.

rhs_question_text: A charity installs a client–server network in a community art centre. Name THREE distinct items of networking hardware, other than the computers and servers, and describe the function of each. [6]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Suitable examples: switch connects devices and forwards frames to recipients; router joins networks and routes data packets; wireless access point allows Wi-Fi clients; NIC connects a device to a network and has a MAC address; Ethernet cable carries signals; bridge joins segments; firewall filters traffic; repeater regenerates a signal.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Three hardware-plus-function pairs at two marks each. A name alone earns one of the pair, development of its actual role earns the other. Total six.

rhs_question_text: An arts centre currently has 150 members and expects membership to grow to 10,000. It must record members, workshop bookings and tutor appointments. Discuss the relative merits of a flat-file and a relational database. Compare their features, advantages and disadvantages, and justify which approach would be more suitable as the centre grows. [9]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Flat files use one table and are straightforward to set up, but repeating members in each booking creates redundancy, update anomalies, slower searches and poor expansion. A relational database uses separate related tables linked through keys, reducing duplication and enabling maintenance, access controls and further tables, but requires design, normalisation and a DBMS. A relational system suits 10,000 members and many bookings better, though a flat file could work initially at 150 members.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Holistic 9-mark teacher assessment: high 7–9 thorough balanced applied comparison and justified conclusion; middle 4–6 sound but underdeveloped; low 1–3 limited; no credit 0.

rhs_question_text:
A wildlife centre stores eight numeric tag IDs in a binary search tree. The root is 50. Its left child is 25 and its right child is 80. Node 25 has left child 10 and right child 40. Node 80 has left child 70 and no right child. Node 40 has left child 35 and right child 45. All other child links are null.

Each node is held in the following fixed 2D-array row order: row 0 is 50; row 1 is 25; row 2 is 10; row 3 is 80; row 4 is 40; row 5 is 45; row 6 is 70; row 7 is 35. The three fields per row are left-index, value and right-index.

Write a valid line of pseudocode or program code declaring an array called nodes with EIGHT rows and THREE columns for this tree representation. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: For example: declare nodes : array[0..7,0..2] of string; or array nodes[8,3]. Equivalent declarations and 7/2 last-index notation accepted.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for valid array declaration named nodes; one for exactly two dimensions of size 8 and 3.

rhs_question_text:
A wildlife centre stores eight numeric tag IDs in a binary search tree. The root is 50. Its left child is 25 and its right child is 80. Node 25 has left child 10 and right child 40. Node 80 has left child 70 and no right child. Node 40 has left child 35 and right child 45. All other child links are null.

Each node is held in the following fixed 2D-array row order: row 0 is 50; row 1 is 25; row 2 is 10; row 3 is 80; row 4 is 40; row 5 is 45; row 6 is 70; row 7 is 35. The three fields per row are left-index, value and right-index.

Complete the blank LEFT and RIGHT fields in this array table, writing null where no child exists. [4]
Index | LEFT | DATA | RIGHT
0 | ? | 50 | ?
1 | ? | 25 | ?
2 | ? | 10 | ?
3 | ? | 80 | ?
4 | ? | 40 | ?
5 | ? | 45 | ?
6 | ? | 70 | ?
7 | ? | 35 | ?
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Four grouped RHS marks: rows 0–1 (1), rows 2–3 (1), rows 4–5 (1), rows 6–7 (1), considering their pointers. Accept -1/empty-marker variants for null consistently. This is an independently numbered example.

rhs_question_text:
A wildlife centre stores eight numeric tag IDs in a binary search tree. The root is 50. Its left child is 25 and its right child is 80. Node 25 has left child 10 and right child 40. Node 80 has left child 70 and no right child. Node 40 has left child 35 and right child 45. All other child links are null.

Each node is held in the following fixed 2D-array row order: row 0 is 50; row 1 is 25; row 2 is 10; row 3 is 80; row 4 is 40; row 5 is 45; row 6 is 70; row 7 is 35. The three fields per row are left-index, value and right-index.

Insert the four new tag IDs 43, 5, 90, 77 into this tree, in that order. For each, state the parent and whether it becomes its left or right child. [4]
rhs_answer_points_draft: 43 is left child of 45; 5 is left child of 10; 90 is right child of 80; 77 is right child of 70.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark per correctly placed node, maximum four. Correct parent and left/right placement required.

rhs_question_text: A drone-maintenance company records quadcopters through an object-oriented class called Drone. Declare FOUR private attributes: serialNo, model, weight and flightTime. Write a public constructor receiving exactly four values and assigning them to the matching attributes. No getter or setter methods are needed. [5]
rhs_answer_points_draft:
One valid model:
class Drone
  private serialNo
  private model
  private weight
  private flightTime
  public procedure new(idIn, modelIn, massIn, timeIn)
    serialNo = idIn
    model = modelIn
    weight = massIn
    flightTime = timeIn
  endprocedure
endclass
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Five marks: suitable class declaration; all four private attributes; public constructor; four appropriate data parameters (implicit self/this not counted); assignments of each parameter to the matching instance field. Accept equivalent valid OOP languages.

rhs_question_text: At a computing-law workshop, learners study the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act and related lawful surveillance authorisations. State THREE different kinds of investigatory access or surveillance powers that qualifying public bodies may be permitted to exercise, subject to legal safeguards. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Indicative categories include interception/monitoring of communications; targeted covert surveillance; lawful demands for communications traffic data; obtaining access to protected data; requiring cooperation with authorised decryption requests. Different statutory authorisations and safeguards apply.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark per different power recognised by the historical OCR scheme, maximum three. Do not describe unrestricted permissions.

rhs_question_text: A charity registers volunteers for events and stores names, contact details and availability. State THREE distinct principles under UK data-protection rules that should guide its handling of personal information. [3]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity/security/confidentiality; accountability.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark per distinct appropriate principle, maximum three. The RHS answer uses modern UK GDPR terms; reconcile with OCR's dated 2024 wording at final source review.
